b: I have worn nearly every hat in the music industry: performer, songwriter, A&R rep, producer, label director, studio owner, and more. But most of what I have done—and loved the most—is making music, and then traveling around performing that music.
If nothing else, it’s a life that is full of stories. And many of those stories have found their way into my collection “Dancing with Poets” directly or tangentially.

Some poems center on people performing music; some on studio engineers or rowdy dive bar audience members; some on instruments; some on particular songs; and some have music in the background, playing from the overhead speakers of our lives.

As I’ve worked to tell these stories, and worked to learn new ways to incorporate music and musical moments into these poems, I’ve found myself seeking poetry that does not approach music as “some vague thing,” but instead operates with the kind of truth that only close-attention is able to arrive at.

What I admire most about each of the collections below is their dedication to detail. Regardless of the author’s own familiarity with the music or musicians, in each collection the author dedicates themselves to the granular, and so is able to access new revelations, and new wonderings, by paying such close attention to music, and the instruments and musicians that make it. These books continue to teach me, in large part, not just how to write about music, but how to pay attention—how to see, and write, the world anew.

Voigt’s Collected is full of music (as subject, as underpinning, as source), but I’ll highlight moments in two sequences which use music—specifically, pianos, and piano playing, as ways to illustrate and embody. From “At the Piano”:

At the piano, the girl, as if rowing upstream,
is driving triplets against the duple meter,
one hand for repetition,
one hand for variation and for song.
She knows nothing, but Bach knows everything.

And here are moments from three sections of Voigt’s Rubato sequence, which (as the quotes hopefully demonstrate) begins with the details of the instrument itself, before moving towards the music and musicians who bring it life, and whose lives are reflected in it.
and here, in section 3, we can witness Voigt play off the piano itself to reveal details of the characters who orbit it:

not what my parents might have played
if my father had ever learned how to play
and if my mother had ever played
anything other than her one song,
And here, in the final section (Section 8), Voigt brings together the biographies, the generations, the physicality of the piano, and the details on music theory and piano performance

…Today, that child turns one
so I play Grieg, her countryman,
then play Schumann’s “Kinderszenen,”
and then: ragtime, American stride left hand
a steady measurement, the free right hand
a stitch ahead of the beat, then a stitch behind,
the stammered math of feeling

Voigt’s use of music is masterful—the poem’s deep knowledge of the instrument, the act of performance, the music being performed, and the playing style and lives of those around the instrument all come together to create a world that is inextricable from the music at the center of it.

Finney’s “Condoleezza Suite” is a sequence of four poems that create a nuanced biography of Condoleezza Rice (as both private and public figure) by detailing Rice’s background as a pianist. Most memorable for me is the way in which Finney identifies physical characteristics of Rice’s playing (in this case—having learned a lineage of music based on major scales that utilize primarily the white keys of the piano, leaving Rice less familiar with stretching to the black keys) as metaphor and image for Rice’s internal life.
These quoted passages come from “Concerto no. 11: Condoleezza and the Chickering”

“When she is a girl she learns to play to the Italian
in her blood…

In the future, when she plays Secretary of State on the
world stage, the black keys will always be a stretch.

When she is at her Watergate window, practicing
at her Chickering, she will, in the tradition of other
deposed heads, refuse to imagine grace notes &
half counts. She won’t, not even when no one is
looking, sideslip or walk the white keys with only
the fingers of her left hand”

What I so admire about Finney’s poetry here is how her attention to detail, and understanding of technical detail, allows her to illustrate an otherwise inaccessible inner world—the Condoleezza Suite becomes a character study, and that study is grounded in the particular as an entryway to the unknown.

Part prose, part poetry, part historical record, part imagined biography, Ondaatje’s Coming Through Slaughter is a book-between-forms centered on Buddy Bolden: the legendary “inventor of jazz” who lived before recording technology existed, and whose life ended in an asylum after a series of mental breaks.

Ondaatje scoured existing historical records to piece together parts of this biography, but did not shy away from invention to bring his version of Bolden, and Bolden’s world, to life. Like Voigt and Finney, Ondaatje is able to reference some distinct pieces of music and compositions as known references. While it may seem Ondaatje’s imagining of Bolden’s life is wildly different from Voigt and Finney’s respective approaches, ultimately I would argue that all of these authors are seeking their own way to create and demonstrate complicated human characters, whether they are linked to historically accurate documents, or exist outside the frame of what is factually known.
Coming through Slaughter defies traditional genre constraints, but the detail of this scene, and how it gives us access to Bolden’s inner life, has stayed with me for decades:

“She was conscious that while they spoke his fingers had been pressing the flesh on her back as though he were plunging them into a cornet. She was sure he was quite unaware, she was sure his mind would not even remember. It was part of a conversation held with himself in his sleep. Even now as she lay against his body in her red sweater and skirt. But she was wrong. He had been improving on Cakewalking Babies.”

What I admire here is not just the attention to detail (in this case, Bolden’s fingers on his lovers back), but how Ondaatje uses this description to reflect how the performer (Bolden) and the listener/receiver (the lover) may view this detail entirely differently—and so reflect the difference in their relation to this music.

Sometimes I find poets are quick to assume they “understand” what a song, or music, or musician is intending with their performance—something I’m sure I’ve been guilty of plenty of times, when one assumes one’s own truth must be “the truth.” But as Ondaatje points out here so exquisitely is that, even if we are feeling the same notes, we may have totally different understandings of where they are coming from.
Rodney Jones, Elegy for the Southern Drawl

If the above examples center on a musician’s relationship with their instrument, Rodney Jones’ Elegy for the Southern Drawl uses “the Southern Drawl” (as speech and sound) as “the instrument” he wishes to detail and elegize. For Jones, music is inseparable from place and from speech, and this collection as well as its titular poem are constantly weaving specific musical references into a tapestry of other notions of place. While it may be more wide-ranging in subject than the previous books in this list, never is Jones vague or general in what he is including—if he is going to talk about music, he is going to name a specific song, or chord. If he is going to talk about landscape, he is going to name the trees, the rivers. Elegy for the Southern Drawl (and its namesake poem) creates its world via palimpsest, which I will attempt to illustrate with these two sections from the poem:

Country songs, sorghum, the odor of lard
That clung to coats, sweat and saliva roaring
Out of the varnish of old desks as the days
Heated up in late spring: it embarrassed me.
And here, in section 9, music and the life of musicians takes center-stage:

Some kind of hippie cowboy on the elevator
Going up in the Music City Day’s Inn,
He’s apologizing for his pink, hard-shell
Guitar case jammed in the closing door,
Thanks, and he’s gone, the only white
Man I’ve heard speaking the hoarse,
Barreled-in English of a native of India…

…This is Nashville,
Shrunken world, a hundred twenty miles
North of home

If Rodney Jones uses musical details and references as one part of a larger “music” of personal and place-specific language, A Van Jordan’s use of music in his collection Rise is often as a particular soundtrack weaving in and out of the speaker’s direct consciousness. While the speakers of the poems in Rise are not musicians themselves, music is essential to the life of those speakers, as is exemplified in a poem like “Public Radio Plays Eddie Harris.” While the poem does not dive into a deep study of Harris or Harris’s saxophone, we understand, through reference and detail, that Harris and Harris’s music are vital to the speaker, and are a companion to the speaker, as the speaker finds his way through the world.

I think this example is crucial among this list because it demonstrates that one does not need to be particularly well-versed in piano construction, or in the multi-generation background of a public figure, in order to successfully incorporate music and musicians into one’s poems. In “Public Radio Plays Eddie Harris,” Jordan provides sufficient detail for us to understand how the speaker feels about Harris, and that is enough to effectively help us (as readers) understand Harris and Harris’s place in this poem:

…If WPFW FM can’t resurrect me, Lazarus was a liar.
Thank God, they’re playing Eddie Harris.
I have friends who are atheists.
I have ammunition for our next argument:
They play four Eddie Harris tunes in a row!
Faith healers are tuning in.
I’m all but cured when they make the announcement:
Eddie Harris died today.
Thoughts tornado over my bed.
It pirouettes over the city with hips like my mama’s.
Eddie always said there’s no such thing as a wrong note,
Only bad connections to the next.
I put the alarm clock under the sheets.
In the morning it will sound like music.
Though not overtly about music as a subject, Dobyns’ Cemetery Nights returns frequently to songs and sounds, perhaps none more clearly than the poem “Loud Music.”

Whereas many of the collections in this list focus on music in its compositions and in the biography of the instruments and musicians, “Loud Music” focuses more on music as sound—and what that sound can be.

Where Rodney Jones incorporates music among a tapestry of personal identity markers, and A Van Jordan writes of Eddie Harris to help us better understand the speaker of his poem, Dobyns’ “Loud Music” shows what a relationship to sound for the sake of sound can be, and what that tells us about the needs of a listener.

My stepdaughter and I circle round and round.
You see, I like the music loud, the speakers
throbbing, jam-packing the room with sound whether
Bach or rock and roll, the volume cranked up so
each bass note is like a hand smacking the gut…

…Loud music does this, it wipes out the ego,
leaving turbulent water and winding road,
a landscape stripped of people and language —
how clear the air becomes, how sharp the colors.

Where Dobyns wishes to obliterate the self with the overwhelm of sound, Ilya Kaminsky, in Deaf Republic, writes of a population that has been obliterated by military occupation, and so becomes deafened—literally refusing their ability to hear—in order to protest, and turn away from the commands of the occupiers.

While all of the collections in this list hold music and sound at its core, Kaminsky builds his book around what happens when that core is removed—in this case, as political protest. What happens when no listening occurs? How does the aggressor demand attention? How do the occupied communicate with one another? What is silence, and what is sound, in a world where some are allowed to shout and others must hold their tongues?
The absence of sound is what Kaminsky’s book is built around, which I’ll quote a few moments from to illustrate how “silence” becomes the central theme:

silence?
it is a stick I beat you with, I beat you with a stick, voice, beat you

until you speak, until you
speak right.
“We are sitting in the audience, still. Silence, like the bullet that’s missed us, spins—
and, from the Notes section at the book’s end (perhaps most tellingly):
ON SILENCE: The deaf don’t believe in silence. Silence is the invention of the hearing.
Dancing with Poets by Reed Turchi is available from University Press of Colorado.
